title: Giant
wpTitle: Giant Reviews Round-up – Starring John Lithgow

ratings.excerpt: John Lithgow shines as the charming monster Roald Dahl … Mark Rosenblatt’s debut play about the complex children’s author is a timely, absorbing piece that surely deserves a bigger stage … Mark Rosenblatt’s debut play about Roald Dahl, best-selling author and unabashed antisemite, is subtle, intelligent and stylishly crafted. With the American star John Lithgow in the lead role and the National’s old boss, Nicholas Hytner, directing, this drama surely deserves a transfer to a bigger stage. … Lithgow is astonishing as the irascible writer rattling around his home in Buckinghamshire. We’ll be lucky to see a better performance this year. Shocking, challenging Roald Dahl play is spectacularly good … Mark Rosenblatt’s fearless script is one thing, but the play about the author’s vile antisemitism is made extraordinary by the performances, led by John Lithgow … Head-on, unflinchingly, Giant confronts the vile antisemitism of one of the most beloved children’s authors of all time, while sweeping along in its ferocious cross-currents of dialogue all the pitched battles of society today: authors with controversial opinions, art versus artist, complicity and silence, the ways we protect the powerful. It’s hard to think when the Royal Court last staged a play that felt so dangerous, or one so spectacularly good. … In a casting coup, John Lithgow plays Dahl, brimful of charm (and he looks uncannily similar to the author. John Lithgow is magnificent as Roald Dahl in Nicholas Hytner’s production of an extraordinary debut play … Here in one evening is the case for the stage. An incendiary subject, an extraordinary debut play, a fleet production, top-notch acting. Everything on the wing. At the centre of Mark Rosenblatt’s Giant towers John Lithgow, magnificent as Roald Dahl: impassioned and soured, mischievous and bullying. … Rachael Stirling brings poised intelligence – askance but not arch – to a finely written part. … Nicholas Hytner’s production has exceptional clarity and conviction, helped by Bob Crowley’s fine design of cluttered (building work is enraging the author) comfort. Exploration of Roald Dahl and antisemitism that speaks to our times … Sophisticated play melds fact with fiction in its dramatisation of a scandalous moment in the life of the author … ... John Lithgow, fabulous, and bearing uncanny resemblance to the writer … ... a slowly brilliant first act, stupendously performed by its cast, which mixes fact with fiction in its dramatisation of a scandalous moment in the life of the children’s writer Roald Dahl. It starts off breezily, heading amblingly into what seems like a middle-class drawing room drama, before becoming as dark and sharp-toothed as one of Dahl’s fictive monsters. … He is no simple monster, though, or at least not in the first act, when he is also rational, tender, likable. A powerful portrait that puts Roald Dahl's uncomfortable views in the dock … At moments last night Lithgow’s brilliantly, brazenly unapologetic performance reduced the theatre to shocked, breathless silence. And he’s a Dahl ringer too. … The play goes off the boil after the interval, but it retains a powerful sense that all the characters are no better or worse than any of us.

John Lithgow is sensational as Roald Dahl in antisemitism drama Giant … This astonishingly good writing debut by longtime director Mark Rosenblatt focuses on the fallout from a review penned by the children’s author … This astonishingly good writing debut by the longtime director focuses on the fallout from a 1983 book review penned by Roald Dahl, the children’s author — played here, sensationally well, by John Lithgow. … Rosenblatt is not unsympathetic towards Dahl, making plain his despair over the suffering of Palestinian children and touching on his personal tragedy (Dahl’s son was brain damaged in a car accident). But he also gives an unflinching account of the author’s blatant antisemitism and capacity for vicious behaviour. It’s a nuanced portrait, intent on unpicking the cognitive

Simmering, tense study of Roald Dahl and antisemitism with a towering turn from John Lithgow … The controversial children’s author is shown to have a bizarre blend of kindness and borderline sadism in Mark Rosenblatt’s debut play, set in 1983 after the publication of ‘The Witches’ and a shocking antisemitic book review … Rosenblatt brilliantly captures the strident, baroquely florid voice of this cantankerous author as he belittles his illustrator Quentin Blake... And Lithgow faultlessly captures Dahl’s bizarre blend of kindness and borderline sadism … ... it’s a play that brings welcome nuance to conversations about antisemitism sparked by the Royal Court’s controversial production of Rare Earth Mettle two years ago – and sketches a memorable portrait of Dahl, one that’s crueller and dark

An enthralling night … Nicholas Hytner’s production is a model of theatrical energy. US star Lithgow is perfect as Dahl, full of pith and vinegar as he spits out terse phrases like poisoned darts while the others duck and weave around him. Rachael Stirling as his inamorata Liccy is posh and conciliatory, Tessa Bonham Jones as Hallie the saucy cook/housekeeper and the ever reliable Levey offer superb support to Lithgow’s monumental performance as the entitled, cantankerous and provocative writer. When Stone and Dahl discover they each have a brain-damaged child, it prompts a rare moment of compassion that suggests Dahl’s abrasive personality is a carapace to protect him from the world – the cruel adult world. An enthralling night.

John Lithgow is a powerful presence as a monstrous Roald Dahl … The first act, directed with classy assurance by Nicholas Hytner (like Lithgow making a much-delayed Royal Court debut), does what good theatre can do better than any other setting, holding and exploring complex, contradictory views without oversimplification. … It’s a play that doesn’t quite decide where it stands in that argument about whether you can loathe the man and admire the art – but thanks to Lithgow, it compels while it is making it.

Cogent depiction of Roald Dahl and his unrepentant glee … The audience is confronted with the full shocking force of Dahl’s anti-Semitism … You have to wait to the final scene of Mark Rosenblatt’s debut play to be confronted with the full shocking force of Dahl’s anti-Semitism, although everything he is quoted as saying here is a matter of public record. Still, for quite a while Rosenblatt attempts, if not to give Dahl the benefit of the doubt, then to at least place his opinions within that old reliable theatrical convention of a back and forth debate round the dinner table. … Lithgow plays Dahl initially as a charming old rogue, all spidery elongated limbs and wire wool hair as though drawn by Quentin Blake himself – yet his unrepentant, raptor-like glee in his untouchable reputation and

Grounded portrait of a larger-than-life figure … Rosenblatt never quite pulls all his threads together – much is left unresolved, and several characters’ arcs are never completed. When their debates get too heated, they politely separate to cool off, dissipating the crackling energy.
